# How to study with this book {.unnumbered}

This page explains *how* the book is organised and *how* to use it to learn
effectively. Read it once; come back to the notation table whenever you meet a
symbol you do not recognise.

## A study method in five steps {.unnumbered}

Research on learning gives a few robust prescriptions. Two of the most
replicated are **retrieval practice** (testing yourself is more effective than
re-reading) and **spacing** (studying the same material in several short
sessions is better than one long session) [@dunlosky2013; @roediger2006].
The book is built around them. For each chapter:

1. **Read the learning objectives.** They tell you what you should be able to
   *do* at the end. If you can already do all of them, skim the chapter.
2. **Read the intuition, then the formal part.** The intuition gives you a
   mental picture; the formal part makes it precise. Do not skip the
   definitions: most mistakes in programming and in mathematics come from a
   vague definition.
3. **Redo the worked examples by hand**, with paper and pencil, *before*
   looking at the solution. Then run the code and compare.
4. **Modify the code.** Change a value, break something on purpose, predict
   what will happen *before* running it. Prediction followed by feedback is
   retrieval practice.
5. **Do the exercises** at the end of the chapter, a day or two later
   (spacing). Solutions are collapsed: open them only after a real attempt.

## Anatomy of a chapter {.unnumbered}

Every chapter follows the same rhythm:

| Section | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Learning objectives** | What you will be able to do. |
| **Intuition** | An everyday picture of the idea, with no formulas. |
| **Theory** | Definitions, theorems, algorithms, with their history and sources. |
| **Worked examples** | Problems solved step by step, by hand. |
| **Practice** | Annotated, runnable code, following the *Practice* lessons of the course. |
| **In the project** | Where and how the chapter is used in the course's final project. |
| **Common pitfalls** | The errors that beginners (and experts) make most often. |
| **Summary** | The ideas to remember. |
| **Exercises** | With collapsed solutions. |
| **Further reading** | An annotated list of the sources, telling you *what to read* in each one. |

## The boxes {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives / Definitions / Notes
Blue boxes contain objectives and important remarks.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Intuition
Green boxes contain intuitions, analogies and tips.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
Orange boxes warn you about pitfalls and frequent misconceptions.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Key result
Red boxes highlight a result you must remember.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## For the interested reader — proofs
Proofs live in collapsed boxes like this one. Each box is **preceded** by a
one-line statement of its result. Open it to see the full derivation.
:::

Theorems, lemmas, definitions, equations, figures and tables are numbered
per chapter — *Theorem 2.3* is the third theorem of Chapter 2 — and every
reference to them is a link, so that a proof can always point precisely to the
results it uses.

## Code and outputs {.unnumbered}

Code cells look like this; the box below the cell shows what Python printed
when the book was built:

```{python}
#| echo: true
greeting = "Hello, AI engineer!"
print(greeting)
```

Some programs need a human at the keyboard (they call `input()`); those cells
are shown but not executed, and a sample session is given as a comment.
Lines starting with `>>>` reproduce an interactive session of the Python
interpreter (the *REPL*, see @sec-repl).

### How to run the code yourself {.unnumbered}

You have two options, both explained in detail in @sec-dev-environment:

- **Google Colab** (nothing to install): open
  <https://colab.research.google.com>, create a notebook, paste a cell, press
  <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Enter</kbd>.
- **Local installation**: install Python 3.13 from <https://www.python.org>,
  then use the REPL, a text editor such as VS Code, or Jupyter.

## Notation {.unnumbered}

| Symbol | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ | natural numbers (we include $0$) | $3 \in \mathbb{N}$ |
| $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$ | integers, rationals, reals | $-2 \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\tfrac12\in\mathbb{Q}$ |
| $x \in A$ | $x$ is an element of the set $A$ | $2 \in \{1,2,3\}$ |
| $A \subseteq B$ | every element of $A$ is in $B$ | $\{1\} \subseteq \{1,2\}$ |
| $A\cup B$, $A\cap B$, $A\setminus B$ | union, intersection, difference | |
| $\lvert A\rvert$ | number of elements of a finite set | $\lvert\{a,b\}\rvert = 2$ |
| $\lfloor x \rfloor$, $\lceil x \rceil$ | floor (round down), ceiling (round up) | $\lfloor 2.7\rfloor = 2$, $\lceil 2.1\rceil=3$ |
| $a \bmod n$ | remainder of the division of $a$ by $n$, in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ | $17 \bmod 5 = 2$ |
| $\log_b x$ | logarithm in base $b$; $\lg x = \log_2 x$, $\ln x = \log_e x$ | $\lg 8 = 3$ |
| $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i$ | $a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n$ | $\sum_{i=1}^{3} i = 6$ |
| $\prod_{i=1}^{n} a_i$ | $a_1 \cdot a_2 \cdots a_n$ | $\prod_{i=1}^{3} i = 6$ |
| $n!$ | factorial, $\prod_{i=1}^{n} i$, with $0! = 1$ | $4! = 24$ |
| $f: A \to B$ | $f$ is a function from $A$ to $B$ | |
| $O, \Omega, \Theta$ | asymptotic bounds (@sec-asymptotic) | $3n^2+n = \Theta(n^2)$ |
| $\Pr[E]$, $\mathbb{E}[X]$ | probability of an event, expectation of a random variable | |
| $\wedge, \vee, \neg$ | logical *and*, *or*, *not* (@sec-boolean-algebra) | $p \wedge \neg q$ |
| $\Rightarrow$, $\Leftrightarrow$ | implies, if and only if | |
| $:=$ | "is defined as" | $\varepsilon := 2^{-52}$ |
| $\blacksquare$ | end of a proof | |

## How references work {.unnumbered}

A citation such as [@knuth1997] or @cormen2022 links to the full entry in the
[References](references.qmd) at the end of the book; hover over it to see the
entry. Each entry gives, whenever they exist, the **DOI** (a permanent
identifier: prefix it with `https://doi.org/` to open the publisher's page),
the **arXiv** identifier for preprints, and a **URL** for standards and
documentation. @sec-finding-sources explains how to obtain each kind of source,
including free legal copies.
